title: I have two siblings
title_target: Έχω δύο αδέρφια — Eh-khoh dhee-oh ah-dhehr-fyah
goal: Say what you have and don't have, give your age, and count to a hundred — including three numbers that change with the gender of the noun.
bekal: build the six forms of έχω
count from zero to a hundred
choose ένας, μία, or ένα correctly

dialogs.title: ΔΙΑΛΟΓΟΣ — Family and age
dialogs.intro: Eleni and Ana chat on the balcony. Notice that the number one changes three times in this dialogue, while the number two doesn't change at all.

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Do you have any brothers or sisters, Ana?

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Yes, I have two: one brother and one sister.
lines.literal: yes, I-have — two: one (masc.) — brother — and — one (fem.) — sister.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: My brother is twenty-five, my sister is eighteen.
lines.literal: the — brother — my — he-is — twenty — five — and — the — sister — my — eighteen.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: I'm twenty-two. How old are you?
lines.literal: I-am — twenty — two. you — how-many — years — you-are?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: Twenty-nine. I only have one sister.
lines.literal: twenty — nine. I-have — only — one (fem.) — sister.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Do you have a house in Athens?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: We have a small apartment here and a house in the village.
lines.literal: we-have — a (neut.) — small — apartment — here — and — a (neut.) — house — in-the — village.

lines.speaker: Άννα:
lines.id: Great! Do you have a car too?

lines.speaker: Ελένη:
lines.id: No, I don't have a car. But I have a motorbike!
lines.literal: no, not — I-have — car. I-have — however — a — motorbike!

notes: **Έχω is an ordinary group A verb** — its endings are exactly the same as μένω from the last unit: έχω, έχεις, έχει, έχουμε, έχετε, έχουν. The only thing to watch is the χ, which isn't h but *kh*, like the *ch* in Scottish *loch*.

⚠️ **Age uses είμαι, not έχω.** *Είμαι είκοσι δύο* — "I am twenty-two". That happens to match English, and differs from French or Spanish, which use "have". If you've learned either of those, watch out: *έχω είκοσι δύο* sounds as if you own twenty-two of something.
**Πόσων χρονών είσαι;** literally means "of how many years are you?". The answer can repeat χρονών or not: *Είμαι είκοσι δύο χρονών* or just *Είκοσι δύο*. The second is heard far more often.

⚠️ **The numbers one, three, and four change with the gender of the noun; the rest don't.** ένας αδερφός, μία αδερφή, ένα σπίτι. τρεις μέρες but τρία παιδιά. τέσσερις ώρες but τέσσερα ευρώ. Twenty-two to a hundred never change again — unless they end in one, three, or four: είκοσι **μία** ώρες.

**Έναν takes a final -ν** when the next word begins with a vowel or one of κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, ξ, ψ: *έναν αδερφό*, *έναν καφέ*. Before other letters the -ν often drops: *ένα φίλο*. ⚠️ When in doubt, write it in full — it's never considered wrong, just slightly more formal.

**Δεν έχω αυτοκίνητο — no article.** When you say you don't have something in general, the noun stands bare, just like English "I don't have a car". Compare: *Δεν έχω **το** αυτοκίνητο* means "I don't have the car", i.e. a specific car already mentioned.
**Όμως (*OH-mohs*, "however") goes in the middle of the sentence**, not at the front like αλλά. *Δεν έχω αυτοκίνητο. Έχω **όμως** μια μηχανή.* The two words sit in different places but mean the same.

⚠️ **Έχω means "have", not "there is".** For "there is / there are", Greek uses **υπάρχει** (*ee-PAHR-khee*): *Υπάρχει μια τράπεζα εδώ κοντά;* — "Is there a bank near here?". The plural is **υπάρχουν**. Translating "there is" with έχω is a classic beginner's slip.

grammars.title: Έχω and the numbers one to twenty
body: You've already mastered έχω if you know the group A endings from the last unit. What's really new here is the numbers — and three of them need attention.
after: Notice that **τρεις** and **τέσσερις** are used for masculine **and** feminine at once; only the neuter form differs. So there are really just two pairs to memorize.

⚠️ **μία** and **μια** are both correct. μία (*MEE-ah*, two syllables) is a bit more emphatic and used when counting; μια (*myah*, one syllable) is used when it means "a / an". In everyday speech, μια wins by a mile.

grammars.title: Zero to a hundred
body: Greek numbers are built exactly like English ones: tens first, then units, with no "and" in between. Είκοσι πέντε = twenty-five. No surprises at all here.
after: Thirteen to nineteen are formed by sticking δεκα- in front: δεκα+τρία → δεκατρία. The only ones that break the pattern are έντεκα (11) and δώδεκα (12), which are older forms — much like English *eleven* and *twelve*.
⚠️ **εφτά / επτά, οχτώ / οκτώ, εννιά / εννέα** — both are used. The first is everyday, the second more formal, and it's the one printed on tickets and notice boards. Recognize both, say the first.

blocks.text: The things most often mentioned in sentences with έχω. Remember: always learn a noun with its article, even though the article is dropped in "don't have" sentences.

blocks.title: Έχω, υπάρχει, and the most common mistake
items: **Έχω** = to have, to have on me. *Έχω δύο αδέρφια.* — I have two siblings.
**Υπάρχει / υπάρχουν** = there is / there are. *Υπάρχει τράπεζα εδώ κοντά;* — Is there a bank near here? *Υπάρχουν πολλά μαγαζιά.* — There are lots of shops.

⚠️ English keeps "have" and "there is" apart, so you start with an advantage. But don't be thrown when you hear *Έχει τράπεζα εδώ;* ("does it have a bank here?") on Greek streets — it's very casual spoken Greek. In exams, in letters, and with people you don't know yet, use υπάρχει.
For "there isn't": **Δεν υπάρχει πρόβλημα** — no problem. This sentence will save you many times over.

exercises.prompt: Add the right ending of έχω.
Put the words in the right order.

items: Is there a shop near here?

answers: Πόσων χρονών είσαι; — Έχω δύο αδέρφια. — Δεν έχω αυτοκίνητο. — Έχω μόνο μία αδερφή. — Υπάρχει τράπεζα εδώ;
Έχω μία αδερφή. — Είμαι είκοσι δύο. — Δεν έχουμε αυτοκίνητο. — Υπάρχει μαγαζί εδώ κοντά; — Έχει τρία παιδιά.
